Formulation
Predisposing: Family history of migraine; possible baseline health anxiety traits.  
Precipitating: Sudden onset severe unilateral headache with visual disturbance and nausea.  
Perpetuating: Ongoing worry about catastrophic causes; physical discomfort reinforcing anxiety.  
Protective: Prompt help-seeking; willingness to follow medical advice.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute migraine with associated anxiety
- Patient Goal(s):
  • Obtain rapid pain relief and clear vision  
  • Ensure condition is not life-threatening
- Clinical Goal(s):
  • Manage migraine symptoms and monitor response  
  • Rule out secondary neurological causes
- Actions (Patient):
  • Take ibuprofen plus anti-emetic as advised; hydrate with sugary carbonated drink  
  • Rest in dark room; limit screen use  
  • Attend same-day in-person appointment for neurological examination; seek urgent care if worsening
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Provide written instructions/prescription for migraine regimen  
  • Conduct neurological examination at scheduled visit  
  • Educate on migraine features, red-flag symptoms, and when to attend ED  
  • Consider escalation to triptan therapy or neurology referral if poor response

Secondary Problem: Health anxiety
- Patient Goal(s):
  • Reduce excessive worry about serious illness  
  • Improve coping when physical symptoms arise
- Clinical Goal(s):
  • Assess severity of health anxiety at follow-up  
  • Provide psychoeducation and consider psychological referral
- Actions (Patient):
  • Keep brief log of headache triggers, symptoms, and anxiety levels  
  • Use relaxation/breathing techniques; limit online symptom searches
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Screen for anxiety disorders at review (e.g., GAD-7, Health Anxiety Inventory)  
  • Offer information on CBT for health anxiety; consider referral to clinical psychologist if persistent

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: Typical migraine presentation, medication options, hydration, red-flag symptoms (sudden neurological deficit, uncontrolled vomiting, worsening pain).
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Escalating pain >10, new weakness/numbness, altered consciousness, persistent vomiting.
- Coping Strategies: Analgesia with anti-emetic, rest in low-stimulus environment, hydration, relaxation techniques.
